title: Temporary materials & dressings
blurb: Dressings, temporary fillings, temporary crowns and temporary cements: why they're needed, which material suits which job, and what to tell the patient.
question: A patient has just had an upper molar prepared for a crown. The permanent crown will come back from the lab in two weeks and will be fitted with resin cement. The dentist asks you to make a temporary crown and choose a temporary cement. What should you prepare, and what should you tell the patient before they leave?

teach.body: A temporary (provisional) restoration or dressing covers a tooth for days or weeks until the definitive restoration can be placed. You'll see them between root canal visits, after a tooth is prepared for a crown, bridge or inlay while the lab makes it, as an emergency cover for a lost filling, and as a soothing dressing for an inflamed pulp. Temporary doesn't mean unimportant: a leaking or broken temporary can let bacteria in, cause pain and let teeth move.

teach.h: What a temporary has to do

children.label: Seal and protect
children.sub: Keeps out bacteria, saliva, hot and cold

children.label: Hold position
children.sub: Stops drifting and over-eruption; keeps the bite

Typical use
Watch out
rows: Sealing a root canal access between visits
Matrix must be made before prep
Weak on purpose, for easy removal
teach.caption: Temporary cements come in eugenol and non-eugenol versions. Choose non-eugenol when the final restoration will be bonded or resin-cemented.

teach.body: A temporary must be easy to place and easy to remove, seal the margins well and be kind to the pulp. It must also last until the next visit. A large temporary filling under heavy biting needs good compressive strength, or it will crack. Any temporary needs some abrasion resistance, or it will wear away within weeks. Front-tooth temporaries also need an acceptable appearance.

steps.label: Pre-op matrix
steps.sub: Impression or vacuum-formed stent BEFORE the tooth is prepared

steps.label: Fill the matrix
steps.sub: Bis-acryl resin into the prepared tooth's space

steps.label: Seat and wait
steps.sub: Over the preparation until it reaches a rubbery set

steps.label: Cement
steps.sub: Thin layer of temporary cement; remove all excess

teach.caption: Leftover cement under the gum irritates it, so excess is cleared carefully, including between the teeth with floss.

teach.h: Advice for a patient with a temporary crown
items: Avoid sticky, chewy and very hard foods; chew on the other side where possible.
Brush gently around it. When flossing, slide the floss out sideways rather than pulling it up, which could lift the crown.
Some sensitivity to hot and cold can be normal.
If it comes off or feels high, keep it and contact the practice promptly: an uncovered tooth can become sensitive and the teeth can move, so the permanent crown no longer fits.

teach.text: If the permanent crown will be fitted with resin cement, the temporary must NOT be cemented with a eugenol cement. Eugenol residue stops resin from setting properly. Choose a non-eugenol temporary cement.

items: Temporaries seal and protect, soothe the pulp, hold tooth position and keep up appearance.
ZOE: sedative dressing and temporary filling; eugenol interferes with resin.
Large temporaries need compressive strength; long-lasting ones need abrasion resistance.
Temporary crowns: pre-op matrix, bis-acryl resin, trim, cement, check bite.
Temporary cement is weak by design; non-eugenol before resin-bonded work.

summary: You can now explain why temporaries and dressings are placed, match ZOE, pre-mixed pastes, glass ionomer, bis-acryl resin and temporary cements to their jobs, link fractured or worn temporaries to compressive strength and abrasion resistance, make and cement a chairside temporary crown in the right order, and give patients clear aftercare advice.

A.q: A temporary filling in a large molar cavity keeps fracturing. Which property should the replacement material have more of?
A.why: Large temporaries under biting load need higher compressive strength to resist crushing forces.

whyNot.0: Translucency is about appearance, not resistance to fracture.
whyNot.1: Radiopacity affects how it shows on a radiograph, not how strong it is.
whyNot.3: Higher thermal conductivity would be worse for the pulp and doesn't add strength.

A.q: The permanent crown will be fitted with resin cement. Which temporary cement is best for the temporary crown?
A.why: Eugenol residue would interfere with the resin cement, so a non-eugenol temporary cement is used.

whyNot.0: Eugenol residue can stop the resin cement setting properly.
whyNot.2: A permanent cement would make the temporary crown very hard to remove.
whyNot.3: Calcium hydroxide is a liner, not a cement for crowns.

A.q: Which is NOT a purpose of a temporary crown?
A.why: A temporary crown is designed to be removed easily at the next visit, so it is never permanently bonded.

whyNot.0: Holding tooth position is a key purpose, so the permanent crown still fits.
whyNot.1: Covering the cut dentine prevents sensitivity and contamination.
whyNot.3: A well-fitting temporary helps keep the gum margins healthy.

B.q: A temporary restoration has worn down noticeably within a few weeks. Which property was lacking?
B.why: Abrasion resistance is the ability to withstand wear from chewing and brushing.

whyNot.0: Working time affects handling during placement, not wear afterwards.
whyNot.2: Colour stability is about staining, not wear.
whyNot.3: Film thickness applies to luting cements, not wear of a filling.

B.q: A patient with an inflamed, aching pulp needs a dressing to settle the tooth before the definitive filling. Which material is most suitable?
B.why: Eugenol is obtundent: it soothes the pulp, so ZOE is the classic sedative dressing.

whyNot.0: Composite is a definitive restoration and has no sedative effect.
whyNot.2: Zinc phosphate is acidic when first placed and can irritate the pulp.
whyNot.3: Amalgam is a permanent filling with no sedative effect.

B.q: What should a patient with a temporary crown be told about flossing?
options: Floss hard to remove any cement
Floss only once it feels loose
B.why: Pulling floss up through the contact can lift the temporary crown, so it is slid out sideways instead.

whyNot.0: Gum health still matters, so gentle flossing is encouraged.
whyNot.1: Forceful flossing could dislodge the temporary crown.
whyNot.3: A loose temporary is a reason to contact the practice, not a trigger to start flossing.

C.q: When is the impression or stent for a chairside temporary crown taken?
options: After the permanent crown is fitted
After the tooth has been prepared
C.why: The matrix records the tooth's original shape, so it is taken before preparation and then used to form the temporary.

whyNot.0: By then the temporary is no longer needed.
whyNot.1: After preparation the tooth's original shape has been lost.
whyNot.3: The temporary is needed on the day of preparation, not at review.

C.q: A dressing is placed between two root canal treatment visits. Which property is most important?
C.why: The dressing must seal well to stop saliva and bacteria re-contaminating the root canals between visits.

whyNot.0: Appearance matters little for a short-term dressing on a back tooth.
whyNot.2: High conductivity is never a desirable property for a dressing.
whyNot.3: Fluoride release is helpful in some materials but sealing the canals is the priority.

C.q: A patient phones to say their temporary crown came off last night. What is the best advice?
options: Leave it out until the fit visit
Keep it and contact the practice
C.why: The tooth should be covered again promptly, as an uncovered tooth can become sensitive and the teeth can move.

whyNot.0: The temporary may be re-cemented, and the tooth shouldn't be left uncovered.
whyNot.1: Leaving it out risks sensitivity and tooth movement, so the permanent crown might not fit.
whyNot.2: Household glue is not safe in the mouth and could harm the tooth and gum.

reteach.title: Think of a temporary like a plaster cast
reteach.question: A plaster cast protects a broken arm until it heals, then it's cut off. How is a temporary restoration the same?

blocks.body: A cast has to be strong enough to protect the arm for weeks, fit snugly so dirt doesn't get in, and come off easily at the end. A temporary is the same: strong enough not to crack (compressive strength), tough enough not to wear through (abrasion resistance), sealed at the edges, and easy to remove when the permanent work is ready. That's why temporary cements are deliberately weak.

blocks.text: A temporary that cracks lacks compressive strength; one that wears away lacks abrasion resistance.

explain.body: Temporaries seal and protect the tooth, soothe an inflamed pulp, hold the tooth's position and bite, and keep up appearance and gum health until the definitive restoration is ready.

test.q: Why does a temporary crown help the permanent crown fit at the next visit?
options: It makes the tooth grow back
test.why: Without a temporary, the prepared tooth and its neighbours can drift or over-erupt, so the lab-made crown may not fit.

whyNot.1: A temporary covers the tooth; it doesn't harden it.
whyNot.2: Temporaries aren't bonded to the neighbouring teeth.
whyNot.3: Lost tooth structure cannot grow back.

explain.body: ZOE for sedative dressings and temporary fillings, pre-mixed moisture-setting paste for sealing root canal access, GIC for longer interim fillings, bis-acryl resin for temporary crowns, and temporary cement to fix them.

test.q: Which material is most often used to make a chairside temporary crown?
test.why: Bis-acryl (composite-type) resin is placed in a pre-op matrix over the prepared tooth to form the temporary crown.

whyNot.0: Alginate is an impression material, sometimes used to make the matrix but not the crown itself.
whyNot.3: Zinc phosphate is a permanent luting cement and base.

explain.body: A large temporary under biting load needs compressive strength or it fractures. Any temporary needs abrasion resistance or it wears away. Pick a stronger material, such as reinforced ZOE or GIC, for larger or longer-term temporaries.

test.q: A temporary in a small cavity is worn almost flat after three weeks. What does this suggest?
test.why: Wear from chewing and brushing shows the material lacks abrasion resistance.

whyNot.0: Fluoride release doesn't cause a material to wear flat.
whyNot.1: Radiopacity is about appearance on radiographs.
whyNot.2: Working time affects placement, not wear afterwards.

explain.body: Take the matrix before preparation, form the crown in bis-acryl resin, trim and polish, cement with temporary cement, remove all excess and check the bite. Use non-eugenol cement if the final crown will be resin-cemented.

test.q: Why is temporary cement deliberately weak?
options: So it sets faster in the mouth
So the crown can be removed easily
So it can be used under composite
test.why: The temporary crown must come off without damaging the tooth when the permanent crown is fitted.

whyNot.0: Strength has nothing to do with eugenol release, and non-eugenol versions exist.
whyNot.1: Weakness isn't related to setting speed.
whyNot.3: Temporary cements are for temporary crowns, not for use under composite.
